ch28.anchor: an expel-the-barbarian man of the National-Learning school
ch28.note: The National Learning (kokugaku) was the nativist scholarship that sought Japan’s pure origins in its oldest texts and shrines, before any Chinese or Western taint. Its more fervent adherents held a “divine-land” faith that reckoned anything foreign a pollution — even a barbarian’s footprint, even a photograph — which is why Itō’s men will not so much as look at the camera.

The chapter ends on the fact. Yamanami, the learned senior man shelved as general secretary and drawn toward Itō, fled the corps in the second month of Keiō 1 (1865). Under the Code he himself had helped frame, desertion meant death: he was brought back and made to cut his belly, with Okita for his second. He was the most famous man the Code destroyed.

ch29.note: Chiba Shūsaku (1792/94–1855) founded the Hokushin Ittō-ryū and, in Edo, the Genbukan, one of the three great sword halls of the day (see ch07). Because the Chiba line stood close to the Mito Tokugawa, the school became a nursery of the domain’s revere-the-Emperor zeal — which is Shiba’s point here: Yamanami came up through it, and his politics came with it.

ch29.anchor: put to death at Tsuruga in Echizen
ch29.note: The Mito Tengu Party (Tengu-tō), the domain’s radical revere-the-Emperor faction, had risen in arms at Mount Tsukuba in 1864 (see ch13). Under Takeda Kōunsai (1803–1865), a former chief councillor of Mito, the survivors marched west to lay their case before Hitotsubashi Yoshinobu in Kyoto and, worn out, surrendered to the Kaga domain late in 1864. The junior councillor Tanuma Genba-no-kami then took charge, stripped and caged the prisoners in Tsuruga’s herring warehouses, and had them beheaded early in 1865: the dead numbered about three hundred and fifty (Shiba’s three hundred and fifty-two; some accounts give three hundred and fifty-three), Kōunsai and his family among them. The standard histories of the Mito rebellion corroborate the event, and reckon the butchery a turning point that swung radical opinion from ‘expel the barbarian’ toward bringing the shogunate down — exactly the shift Shiba marks in this chapter.

Beien, ‘rice and salt’, is a set phrase for the bare means of living; the Shinsengumi drew its keep from the shogunate. Yamanami’s revulsion is at eating the bread of the power that had just slaughtered men of his own persuasion.

ch29.anchor: hail fell about one sun across
ch29.note: A sun is an old unit of about three centimeters, a little over an inch; hail that size is a tall tale of the northern winters — the harmless, homesick sort of boast a doomed man falls back on when he will not speak of what waits for him.

ch29.anchor: A courtesan of Shimabara named Akesato
ch29.note: The scene that follows — the woman at the lattice, the small feet — is among the most famous in Shinsengumi lore, but it rests on a single late source, the popular chronicler Shimozawa Kan, and no register of the Shimabara quarter records a courtesan of this name in these years. Many historians doubt that Akesato existed at all. Shiba, writing a novel, keeps the cherished tradition; the reader should hold it as legend, not record.

ch29.anchor: the black-lacquered fair-weather clogs and the white tabi
ch29.note: Hiyori-geta are low lacquered clogs on shallow teeth, worn on fine days (the name means ‘fair-weather clogs’); tabi are the split-toed cloth socks worn with them. That Okita takes in only the footwear — not the weeping face he will not raise his eyes to — is how the passage carries the weight of what he is about to do.

ch30.anchor: take supreme command of the Second Chōshū Expedition
ch30.note: The first expedition of 1864 (see ch27) had ended almost without fighting when Chōshū feigned submission and beheaded three of its elders. This second expedition, decreed in 1865, was another matter: the domain had swung back to its radicals and rearmed, and, as Shiba says, the shogunate had neither the money, the strength, nor a lawful pretext for it. The Shogun Iemochi came up to command it in person, fell ill at Osaka Castle, and died there in 1866 as the campaign went against him — the war that broke the Tokugawa. The account is historically accurate.

The uma-jirushi was the tall battle-standard that marked a commander’s place in the field. The golden fan had been the Tokugawa house’s device since Ieyasu; to see it carried into Kyōto was to see the shogun come in war-array, which is why the townsmen read it as a show of power restored.

ch30.anchor: the kind of sacred palanquin was different
ch30.note: The whole knot of the age in one image. Kondō and Itō both revere Kusunoki Masashige (see ch12), the model of the loyal vassal — but Kondō’s loyalty runs to the shogun and Itō’s to the Emperor, so the same hero is borne, as it were, in two different palanquins. Toshizō sees that men on the same side already march under opposed flags.

Napoleon III, emperor of the French, backed the shogunate through his minister Léon Roches with loans and arms and a scheme to remodel its forces on the French pattern (see ch27). Shiba’s aside looks ahead: this same emperor would be captured at Sedan in 1870 and his throne fall, so that the shogunate had staked its revival on a patron about to lose his own. The forward glance is accurate.

The secret compact by which Satsuma and Chōshū, until then at each other’s throats, agreed to make common cause against the shogunate. Brokered by the Tosa men Sakamoto Ryōma and Nakaoka Shintarō, it was sealed at Kyōto early in 1866, joining Saigō Takamori of Satsuma and Kido Takayoshi — the Katsura Kogorō of this book — of Chōshū. It is the hinge on which the Restoration turns, and, as Shiba stresses, the Shinsengumi, whose whole business was to police Kyōto for the shogunate, never suspected it. (Ryōma’s band, the Kaientai from 1867, was at this date still his Nagasaki company, the Kameyama Shachū; Shiba uses the later name.)

ch30.anchor: the French system of army organization
ch30.note: The corps was recast on Western lines: the old rank of jokin (roughly, officer) was dropped, and ten numbered units under captains put in its place, in imitation of the shogunate’s newly French-drilled infantry. The new post of staff officer (sanbō) given to Itō was, like Yamanami’s old ‘general secretary,’ a grand title with no troops under it. Toshizō kept the real command as vice-commander, and had drawn the whole roster to seat Itō’s faction where it could do least harm.

ch30.anchor: and I'd fain drink long (Chōshū) and deep.
ch30.note: A street lampoon (rakushu) built on two puns the parentheses gloss: kyatsu, ‘that fellow,’ for Aizu, the domain then holding Kyōto, and nagashi, ‘long,’ for Chōshū. The conceit is a wife-swap — cast off the Aizu spouse, take a better, and drink deep with Chōshū — and it measures how the capital’s sympathy had turned from the shogunate’s enforcers toward the beaten domain.

ch30.anchor: Hurrying toward home, the clouds of the Fifth Month.
ch30.note: The joke Okita catches: satsuki-gumo, ‘clouds of the Fifth Month,’ is a summer season-word (kigo), yet Toshizō writes it in the eleventh month, deep in autumn. He would sooner have the bright summer word than a lonely autumn one — a small window, as Okita sees, onto the homesick heart beneath the cold enforcer. Toshizō signs his verse Hōgyoku (see ch19).

Nagai Naomune (1816–1891), a senior shogunal official; here Grand Inspector (ōmetsuke), the office set to watch the daimyō. Late in 1865 he led an embassy to Hiroshima to interrogate Chōshū over the coming war, and Kondō, Itō, and two others rode in his train — Kondō under the borrowed name Kondō Kuranosuke. The mission is historical; the Chōshū side, as Shiba says, sent a stand-in envoy and never meant to treat.

ch31.anchor: went also by the name of Fudōdō-mura
ch31.note: The corps’s grandest and last barracks, at Fudōdō-mura by Shichijō-Horikawa, a walled compound with a drill-ground, said to have housed some two hundred men. Historically the Shinsengumi did not move there until 1867 (before that they were billeted at the Nishi-Honganji); Shiba brings the move forward to set this night here.

The Kōnoike were the richest merchant-bankers of Osaka, lenders to daimyō and shogunate alike (see ch15). Self-styled loyalist rōnin preyed on such houses with forced ‘war-chest’ loans; to be rid of them the Kōnoike paid the Shinsengumi for protection, and the money went, as Shiba notes with some dryness, into Kondō’s pleasures. It is a small clear picture of how the corps was kept.

Ōtani Yoshitsugu (1559–1600), Hideyoshi’s able and much-loved general, later a stalwart of the losing side at Sekigahara. A famous anecdote has Hideyoshi say that he should like to give Ōtani a hundred thousand men and watch him wield them — the highest praise for a commander’s grip on a great army. For the Aizu officer to reach for it in speaking of Toshizō is to rank his generalship above Kondō’s.

ch32.note: The Totsukawa-gō was a mountain district of Yamato (modern Nara) whose gōshi, or rural samurai, held in return for old service a rare exemption from tax and a fierce, hereditary loyalty to the Emperor. Many came up to Kyōto as the Restoration neared — Totsukawa men had risen with the Tenchūgumi in 1863 — which is why one of them stands here among Shichiri’s hired swords.

Tanaka Mitsuaki (1843–1939), a Tosa loyalist who after the Restoration rose to count and Imperial Household Minister and made himself the great collector of the Restoration men’s records. Shiba breaks his own narrative to quote Tanaka’s recollection — the enemy’s own testimony to how the mere sight of Hijikata scattered the young loyalists — a real memoir set down in old age, long after the event.

A gandō was a hand-lantern with its candle hung in gimbals inside a hooded metal barrel, so that it stayed lit at any angle and threw its beam one way only, like a bull’s-eye lamp — the night-fighter’s and the housebreaker’s light.

ch32.anchor: the left-mitsudomoe crest on Toshizō's right sleeve
ch32.note: The mitsudomoe is a whirl of three comma-shapes, an old and common device; the ‘left’ form turns one way, the ‘right’ the other. This left-mitsudomoe was the Hijikata family crest. That the dead husband’s clothes Oyuki later brings out bear the very same crest is the quiet omen Shiba sets at their meeting.

None of this is history. Oyuki is Shiba’s one wholly invented character; in his afterword he says he made her up, to give Toshizō a private life the record does not supply, and so a door into the man’s inward self. The circumstantial detail — the art-name Kōka, the surviving paintings, the teacher Yoshida Ryōdō, the Ōgaki husband — is the novelist’s craft, not fact: there was no historical Oyuki. She recurs to the end of the book.

ch33.anchor: the fleet of four nations in the Bakan Strait
ch33.note: In 1863 Chōshū, obeying the Court’s order to expel the barbarian, had fired on foreign ships passing the Shimonoseki (Bakan) Strait. The reply came in the eighth month of 1864, when a combined fleet of Britain, France, the United States, and the Netherlands bombarded and stormed the Shimonoseki batteries and reduced them to ruin. It was the one time a single domain made war on the Western powers alone, and Itō turns it here to Chōshū’s credit. Historically accurate.

ch33.anchor: a direct retainer of the shogun's house
ch33.note: To be made a jikisan was to become a direct retainer of the shogun — a hatamoto or lesser bannerman of the Tokugawa house itself (see ch02), not the vassal of some provincial lord. The wooing begun here bore fruit: in 1867 the Shinsengumi was in fact raised as a body into the shogunate’s direct service, and Kondō given the standing of a hatamoto. For a band of masterless men it was a startling elevation — and, as Toshizō sees, it forced the break with Itō’s faction, who had deserted their lords precisely so as not to serve one again.

Itō appeals to sokuin no jō, the ‘heart of compassion’ that the philosopher Mencius named as the seed of humaneness — the reflex that makes one start to a child about to fall into a well. Rendered into a warrior’s idiom it becomes bushi no nasake, the mercy a samurai owes a beaten foe: to strike Chōshū while it lies wounded, Itō argues, is to forfeit that, and with it the name of samurai.

ch34.anchor: Sennyū-ji in the eastern hills of Kyoto
ch34.note: Sennyū-ji, in Kyoto’s Higashiyama, had been the mortuary temple of the imperial house since the thirteenth century, the emperors’ graves lying within its grounds; Kaikō-ji is one of its sub-temples. The meeting-place looks ahead: when Itō’s men formally left the Shinsengumi in the spring of 1867 they styled themselves the Goryō-eji, the ‘Guards of the Imperial Tombs,’ nominally charged with tending these very graves (Emperor Kōmei had just been buried here). Historically grounded.

ch34.anchor: but will the wholesaler sell it that cheap?
ch34.note: Shinohara plays on a proverb, sō wa ton’ya ga orosanai — literally ‘the wholesaler won’t let it go at that price,’ meaning ‘it won’t be that easy.’ He then turns the merchant image into the figure that runs through the chapter: Toshizō is the okeya, the cooper, who binds the loose staves of the corps into one tub with hoops no shock can spring. The pun linking the two tradesmen does not survive into English.

ch34.anchor: the man later known as Kirino Toshiaki
ch34.note: Nakamura Hanjirō took the name Kirino Toshiaki after the Restoration. It is a pointed pairing: the Satsuma man-cutter who steers Itō toward the imperial party here would end, like Saigō, in revolt against the very government he helped to make, dying at Shiroyama in 1877.

Hijikata really did keep a book of haiku under the pen-name Hōgyoku; some forty-one verses survive as the Hōgyoku hokku-shū, compiled in the spring of 1863 before he went up to Kyoto and now held at the Hijikata Toshizō Museum in Hino. The preponderance of spring poems, and of plum blossom, is genuine. Corroborated.

Gidayū-bushi, the dramatic sung narration of the puppet theatre and the kabuki stage, named for the chanter Takemoto Gidayū (1651–1714); a taste for it marks Toshizō as a man of the Edo-country townsman’s world, not the schooled samurai’s.

ch34.anchor: that sold saké and sweet saké
ch34.note: The ‘sweet saké’ is amazake, a thick, barely alcoholic drink of fermented rice, served warm and sold at night-stalls; that Toshizō asks for it in place of wine is what draws Shichiri’s sneer, ‘how gentle of you.’

ch34.anchor: he had loosened his blade in its scabbard
ch34.note: To ‘cut the carp’s mouth’ (koiguchi o kiru) is to break the sword free of the tight fit where the guard meets the scabbard mouth — the first motion of a draw. Done idly, with a laugh, it is a silent threat.

A gō-ō pledge-sheet issued by the Kumano shrines, printed over with the crows sacred to their gods; to swear on one and break the oath was held to call down divine punishment. Shichiri’s calling it ‘old-fashioned’ is the joke of a man who no longer quite believes in it.

Yadake, a slender, hard bamboo whose straight canes were cut for arrow-shafts; a warrior household grew a stand of it as both material and emblem. The farm boy’s planting it, in longing to be a samurai, is preserved in the Hijikata family traditions.

ch35.anchor: one plank bridge, with neither railing nor handrail
ch35.note: The bridge at Nijō in those years crossed the Kamo in two spans, resting midstream on a nakasu, a grassy sandbar — the ‘Nijō Nakasu’ of the chapter title. The river has since been narrowed and embanked and the sandbar is gone; the modern Nijō-ōhashi is a single span.

Tenchū, ‘the chastisement of Heaven,’ was the slogan under which loyalist swordsmen in these years murdered officials, merchants, and rival activists, often pinning a placard on the body to justify the killing as a public execution rather than a private one. Kennosuke, below, boasts of just such a tally.

Konnyaku (konjac) is a firm, near-tasteless jelly made from the corm of the devil’s-tongue plant, about as bland a food as a Japanese kitchen offers. ‘A man who will take neither vinegar nor konjac’ is a proverb for one so contrary that nothing whatever will move him.

ch35.anchor: served, too, as a constable's informer
ch35.note: A meakashi: a commoner, very often a reformed gambler or ex-convict, employed off the books by the town constables as a thief-taker and informer. Yohei’s past explains why he can read Toshizō’s trade at a glance and why his blood is up.

Hitokiri, ‘man-cutter’: the era’s word for its political assassins, a handful of whom (Kirino among them, see ch34) became legends. Shichiri claims the title for himself; the boast of a private count of the dead was itself a mark of the type.

ch35.anchor: whipped a tasuki round to bind back his sleeves
ch35.note: A tasuki is a cord looped across the back and over both shoulders to gather the long kimono sleeves out of the way of the arms; a swordsman going into a fight tied one on, here improvised from the sageo, the cord that secures the scabbard at the belt.

ch35.anchor: exposed the head on a stake
ch35.note: Sarashi-kubi: the severed head set on a spike at a public place beside a written placard naming the dead man’s offense. It was the ordinary end the loyalist bands meted out to those they killed, and the fate Toshizō grants he himself only just escaped.

Daikon, the big white radish: as a term of contempt it means a duffer, a nobody — used of a wooden actor or, as here, of a swordsman reckoned no threat. Shichiri had sold Toshizō to his hirelings as an easy kill.

ch36.anchor: a corps banner with the chrysanthemum crest
ch36.note: The sixteen-petalled chrysanthemum is the crest of the imperial house; to fly it was to claim the Court’s own sanction. Itō’s faction left the Shinsengumi on the tenth of the third month of Keiō 3 (14 April 1867), a month after the death of the Emperor Kōmei, and took the commission of Goryō-eji, guards of that emperor’s tomb at Sennyū-ji — the very temple where the plot was hatched (ch34). They based themselves at Kōdai-ji. The dates are historically exact. The breach ran to its end at Aburanokōji in the eleventh month of the same year, where Kondō had Itō killed.

‘Tōshō Daigongen,’ the Great Avatar Shining over the East, was the divine title under which Tokugawa Ieyasu was enshrined at Nikkō after his death in 1616. Kondō’s argument is that the shogun’s office of sei-i taishōgun — ‘great general who quells the barbarians’ — was itself conferred by the Court, so that to serve the shogunate is to serve the Throne; Itō hears in it only a man who has swallowed the shogunate’s case whole.

ch36.anchor: a stray by-blow of Lord Tōdō
ch36.note: Lord Tōdō was the daimyō of Tsu, in Ise. The tale that Heisuke was his unacknowledged son is a tradition attached to him and not established fact; Shiba gives it as legend, and it colors the townsman’s touchiness about being taken for a mere farmer’s recruit.

ch36.anchor: the singing of a hauling-chant in the timber-yards
ch36.note: Kiyari: the rhythmic work-song by which gangs of laborers hauled great timbers or raised heavy weights together, a sound of the Edo townsman’s trades — and, sung by firemen, a mark of the swaggering iki style. Fukagawa, across the river, was Edo’s great lumber district.

ch36.anchor: a May wind blowing clean through his belly
ch36.note: An idiom for an open, uncomplicated, empty-headed nature: as though nothing weighed inside a man but a light spring breeze. That even so breezy a soul as Heisuke had turned to the loyalist cause is Toshizō’s measure of how the times were running.

ch36.anchor: A memoir of that night by Shinohara Tainoshin
ch36.note: Shinohara’s written reminiscences are a genuine source for the split, and Shiba quotes them here (with his own bracketed glosses) in their stiff classical Japanese. That the memoirist boasts of having gone resolved to kill Kondō and Hijikata, and been given no opening, is a self-portrait to weigh accordingly — the loser’s account of a quarrel he lost.

ch36.anchor: killed him outright with a single stroke
ch36.note: The killing of Takeda Kanryōsai by Saitō Hajime on the Takeda road is historical, in the sixth month of 1867; Takeda, drifting toward Satsuma, was cut down as a deserter under the corps law. The scene stands as Kondō and Hijikata’s wordless reply to Itō’s faction. Corroborated.

ch37.anchor: an Edo foot-guard permanently stationed in the city
ch37.note: An okachi was a foot-soldier retainer of the shogun, the lowest rank of direct vassal, who went on foot where mounted men rode; jōfu means his post kept him permanently in Edo rather than rotating to a lord’s home province. Oyuki is thus of low but genuine Edo samurai stock — the source of the crisp, unsoftened Edo speech that so draws Toshizō.

That Satsuma’s two coming giants, Ōkubo and Nakamura Hanjirō (Kirino), personally cultivated Itō’s little band measures how seriously Satsuma took it: not as ideological friends but as a ready-made strike force inside Kyoto, to be spent when the day came. Historically grounded.

ch37.anchor: a captain of a Great-Guard unit
ch37.note: The ōgoban, the Great Guard, was one of the shogunate’s standing military corps of hatamoto. In the sixth month of 1867 the whole Shinsengumi was taken into direct shogunal service and its leaders given Great-Guard rank — Kondō as a unit commander, Hijikata as a captain. For men born to farming families it was a startling rise, and it is the ‘risen in the world’ that Oyuki gently needles him about. Historically accurate.

ch37.anchor: would have looked down on the samurai of the domains
ch37.note: The distinction is between a jikisan or direct retainer of the shogun (see ch33) and a baishin, a ‘rear-vassal’ — the retainer of some daimyō, and so only the shogun’s vassal’s vassal. Even a common Shinsengumi trooper, now a direct retainer, outranked in theory the samurai of the great domains; the lowest of them fell below omemie, the privilege of being received in the shogun’s presence.

Mokuroku, ‘the catalogue,’ was a middle license in a sword school, above the beginner’s kirigami and below full menkyō; it certified that the pupil had been shown the school’s recorded techniques. Toshizō’s doctor-brother had reached it as a boy under Kondō’s adoptive father.

Rai San’yō (1780–1832), poet and historian, whose Nihon Gaishi (see ch30) shaped the loyalist imagination of the age; to write ‘in the manner of San’yō’ is to write Chinese-style verse in his admired, vigorous mode.

Tatami-iwashi: tiny whitebait spread in a lattice and dried into a thin, crackling sheet, toasted and eaten as a relish — a homely Edo food. That Oyuki asks for it, and colors as she does, is the whole of her homesickness in one word, and it is her Edo-ness Toshizō loves.

ch38.anchor: billeted ahead and lodge at the honjin
ch38.note: A honjin was the official inn of a post-station on the great highways, reserved for daimyō, court nobles, and high shogunal officials on their journeys; quarters were booked ahead by billeting-men, and a wooden placard (sekifuda) naming the lodger was hung at the gate. For a farmer’s son to travel so, with a name-board of his own, is the whole comedy of the chapter’s opening.

ch38.anchor: the site of the Naval Drill Ground at Teppōzu
ch38.note: The signs of the opening country were rising in Edo itself: a school for training with foreigners by the Hitotsubashi gate, and, on the old naval ground at Teppōzu (Tsukiji), the Tsukiji Hotel, Japan’s first Western-style hotel, begun in 1867 for the foreign residents the treaties now admitted. Historically grounded.

The Kiheitai, ‘irregular militia,’ was the mixed-class volunteer corps raised in Chōshū by Takasugi Shinsaku in 1863, open to farmers and townsmen alongside samurai; drilled in Western style, it became the backbone of Chōshū’s new army. Toshizō wants the same raw material for the same reason — that men with a stipend to lose no longer fight.

An anpotsu-kago was a heavier, better-appointed palanquin than the open town kind, one that sumptuary custom reserved to samurai households of standing. That Toshizō arrives home in one is exactly the ‘stiff neck’ the Hino folk resent.

Ishida sanyaku, ‘Ishida Powder,’ was a real folk remedy for bruises and sprains compounded by the Hijikata family of Ishida village and hawked from village to village — the trade the boy Toshizō carried on his own back. Koryōsan, ‘consumption powder,’ was another family preparation; that it could do nothing for Okita’s tuberculosis makes Toshizō’s faith in it the more affecting.

ch38.anchor: returned the government to the throne
ch38.note: The Taisei Hōkan: on the fourteenth of the tenth month of Keiō 3 (9 November 1867) the shogun Tokugawa Yoshinobu formally offered to return the governing power to the imperial Court, and it was accepted the next day — ending, on paper, two and a half centuries of Tokugawa rule. Toshizō sets out to recruit for a shogunate that has, unknown to him, just surrendered its authority; the news reaches him only at Odawara. Historically exact.

The phrase renders nishiki o kazaru, ‘to deck oneself in brocade’ — from an old Chinese saying that to win success and not return home to be seen in it is like walking abroad by night in embroidered silk. Hikogorō means that Toshizō owes the home country the sight of his success; Toshizō, characteristically, will not perform it.

ch39.anchor: the eighteenth of the eleventh month, in the third year of Keiō
ch39.note: The Aburanokōji Incident. The lunar date Keiō 3/11/18 converts to 13 December 1867. Kondō lured Itō to his residence, plied him with drink, and had him speared and cut down on his way home near the Aburanokōji; the corps then left the body as bait and ambushed the Goryō-eji who came to recover it, killing Tōdō Heisuke, Hattori Takeo, and Mōnai (Kenmotsu). The novel makes the swordsman who finished Itō one Mutō Katsuzō; other accounts name Ōishi Kuwajirō among the assassins. The sequence of events is well attested.

Sei-i Taishōgun, 'Great General who Subdues the Barbarians,' the full title of which 'shogun' is the everyday abbreviation. First given to commanders sent against the Emishi of the north, it became from the twelfth century the title of the hereditary military ruler of Japan.

Minamoto no Yoritomo (1147–1199), founder of the Kamakura shogunate and the first warrior to rule Japan as Sei-i Taishōgun. Kondō's point is that a warrior house had held real power for the near seven centuries since.

Yoshitsune (1159–1189), Yoritomo's younger half-brother and the most dazzling commander of the Genpei War, hunted to his death by the very brother he had won the war for. He is the proverbial beautiful, doomed, melancholy hero — hence Toshizō's jibe about a chief who broods 'with a pale face like some Yoshitsune.'
Mount Tai (Taizan) in Shandong, foremost of China's five sacred peaks and a stock image for massive, unshakable steadiness.

The Western folding umbrella (kōmori-gasa, 'bat umbrella'), so named for its black ribs and cloth. A novelty of the treaty-port years; that hatamoto and then townsmen were carrying it marks how fast Edo was Westernizing by 1867.

ch39.anchor: There were no fireworks at Ryōgoku this year
ch39.note: The summer fireworks over the Sumida River at Ryōgoku Bridge had been an Edo institution since the 1730s. Their cancellation registers the unsettled, money-short mood of the capital in the last year of the shogunate.

Jōfu: retainers of a domain posted permanently to Edo rather than rotating home under the alternate-attendance system. Their children were Edo-born and Edo-bred, which is why Nagakura's homesickness for the city runs deeper than the others'.

ch39.anchor: he changed his name to Kashitarō to mark it
ch39.note: Itō took the name Kashitarō (甲子太郎) to commemorate the sexagenary year kinoe-ne (1864) in which he joined the Shinsengumi; on defecting to Satsuma he changed it again, to Settsu. The serial renaming, the narrator notes, was peculiarly his own habit.
The Noh play Chikubushima, named for the island shrine of the goddess Benzaiten in Lake Biwa. That Itō is cut off mid-chant lends the killing its theatrical hush.

ch40.anchor: unmoving as a mountain, unhurried as a forest
ch40.note: An echo of Sun Tzu — 'swift as the wind, quiet as the forest, fierce as fire, immovable as the mountain' — the maxim Takeda Shingen bore on his war-banner (fū-rin-ka-zan). It is Toshizō's ideal for the corps, and he quotes another strain of it aloud a few lines on.

Toshizō names the standard reading of a half-schooled samurai: the Analects of Confucius and the Mencius; the Jūhasshiryaku, a Yuan-dynasty digest of Chinese history long used as a Japanese primer; and the Nihon Gaishi, Rai San'yō's popular history of the warrior houses.
The two Chinese classics of war: the Sunzi (Sun Tzu's Art of War) and the Wuzi, ascribed to the general Wu Qi. Toshizō prefers these books of pure tactics to the moralizing histories.

ch40.anchor: the way a bystander reads a game of go
ch40.note: From the proverb okame-hachimoku: the onlooker at a game of go sees eight moves further than the players absorbed in it. Toshizō means that book-learning only sets a man second-guessing his own resolve.

ch40.anchor: on the second day of the fifth month of the thirty-first year of Meiji
ch40.note: That is, 2 May 1898. Yoshinobu (1837–1913) lived out his thirty-year retirement in near-total seclusion and was only then received again by the Emperor Meiji — the measure, for Shiba, of the completeness of his self-effacement.

ch41.anchor: boasted the authority of the Tokugawa
ch41.note: The Fushimi Magistracy (bugyōsho), the shogunate's administrative and judicial seat for the Fushimi post-town and its river port south of Kyoto. Its walled compound made a natural forward strongpoint; the next chapter finds the site built over as a housing estate.

The nine gates (kumon) of the outer enclosure of the Kyoto palace. To be commanded to guard them was to be received back as a trusted Imperial force — a total reversal of Chōshū's disgrace after the Hamaguri Gate affair of 1864, and a sign of how far Satsuma had turned the court.

The Minié rifle, a muzzle-loader firing the expanding conical Minié ball; its rifled barrel gave range and accuracy far beyond the old smoothbore musket. Its spread is the material fact behind Chōshū's transformation in four years.
The 'four-kin' (yonkin) gun, a light rifled field piece throwing roughly a four-pound shell — the modern French-derived artillery of the new-model armies, outranging the shogunal side's smoothbores.
The Geweer (Japanese geberu), a Dutch smoothbore percussion musket without even a rear sight: obsolete beside the rifled Minié, and typical of the shogunal side's mixed, dated equipment.

A married woman of the townsman and samurai classes shaved her eyebrows (and blackened her teeth); unshaved brows mark this woman as keeping the presentation of a maiden or an independent widow rather than a matron. Toshizō is describing Oyuki, a samurai widow.

ch42.anchor: turned again at the Battle of Toba-Fushimi
ch42.note: The Battle of Toba-Fushimi (Keiō 4/1/3–6, i.e. 27–30 January 1868), the opening clash of the Boshin War, fought on the roads into Kyoto from the south. Though heavily outnumbered, the Satsuma-Chōshū forces broke the shogunal army; when the Imperial brocade banner was raised, the Tokugawa side became 'rebels,' and the campaign was decided. Well attested.
The battle of Sekigahara (1600), at which Tokugawa Ieyasu's victory made him master of Japan and founded the order that Toba-Fushimi would bring down.

Matsumoto Ryōjun (1832–1907), later Matsumoto Jun: shogunal physician, pupil of the Dutch doctor Pompe, founder of Japan's first Western hospital at Nagasaki, and after the Restoration the army's first surgeon-general and a baron. Shiba's aside that he opened Japan's first sea-bathing beach is right in substance but wrong in place — the beach was at Ōiso (1885), not Zushi, as the author's own hedge, 'Zushi, I believe,' half-concedes.
J. L. C. Pompe van Meerdervoort (1829–1908), the Dutch naval surgeon who from 1857 gave Japan its first systematic instruction in Western medicine, at Nagasaki.
Hōgen ('Eye of the Law'), in origin a Buddhist clerical rank, was granted by the court as an honorary title to eminent physicians, painters, and other men of skill.

ch42.anchor: the Winter and Summer Sieges of Osaka
ch42.note: The two campaigns of 1614–15 in which Ieyasu manufactured pretexts to destroy the Toyotomi house — reduced by then to a single great domain at Osaka — that his own overlord's heir, Hideyori, still headed. Toshizō sees the same maneuver being worked on the Tokugawa now, and in the same castle.

Mitogaku, the historiography built around the Dai Nihonshi compiled by the Mito Tokugawa, which judged the past by loyalty to the throne and branded the disloyal 'enemies of the Court.' Yoshinobu, a Mito son, could not bear to wear that name — the flaw, Shiba argues, that unmanned him.

The tōsatsu-hyō, the manifesto under which the shogunal army marched on Kyoto, cast as a petition to the throne against the Satsuma 'traitors.' By 'rising to the challenge' with it, the Tokugawa side gave Satsuma exactly the war it wanted.

ch43.anchor: which one might call a second Warring-States age in the nation
ch43.note: 'Boshin' is the sexagenary name of the year 1868 (Keiō 4 / Meiji 1), and the war that opens here is named from it. Shiba's 'second Warring-States age' looks back to the century of sixteenth-century civil war that Ieyasu had ended.
The shirasu, the white-graveled forecourt of a magistracy, where the accused knelt and sentence was pronounced — a fitting seat for the corps that had policed Kyoto by the sword.

The corps' own standard bore the single character makoto ('sincerity'). Over it they now flew the Rising-Sun ensign as the flag of the whole shogunal army, in the conviction that theirs was Japan's lawful government. The claim would collapse within days: once the Imperial brocade banner (nishiki no mihata) was carried over the Satsuma-Chōshū side, the Tokugawa army became, in law, a rebel host.

ch43.anchor: commander of the Fourth Army in the Russo-Japanese War
ch43.note: Nozu Michitsura (1841–1908) rose to field marshal and commanded the Fourth Army against Russia in 1904–05; his elder brother Shizuo, the outpost captain here, also became a general. Shiba's habit of flashing forward to these junior officers' later eminence measures how many of Meiji's commanders were blooded at Toba-Fushimi.

Ōyama Iwao (1842–1916), the young Satsuma gunner on Ryūunji-yama, became army minister, field marshal, and commander-in-chief of the Manchurian armies against Russia — one of the towering figures of the Meiji state.

The Asobi (elsewhere the ju) were the neighborhood bands into which the sons of upper Aizu samurai were grouped from about age six; each afternoon's meeting opened with the recited code Shiba gives here, which in its full form ended with the famous line, 'What must not be done, must not be done.' It bred the ferocious discipline that would make Aizu's stand — and its tragedy — in this war.
The Naganuma-ryū of military science (gungaku), the tradition of tactics and drill in which the Aizu domain trained its troops.

ch43.anchor: the Great Elder of the shogunal council
ch43.note: The tairō ('Great Elder'), the highest office of the shogunate, filled only in a crisis and by custom from a few premier hereditary houses — the Ii of Hikone chief among them, whose Ii Naosuke had held it at the time of the Perry treaties. Their going over to Satsuma is thus a defection of the Tokugawa vanguard itself.

ch43.anchor: became the first shot of the Battle of Toba-Fushimi
ch43.note: The shell from Nozu's Satsuma battery, fired about 5 p.m. on Keiō 4/1/3 (27 January 1868), was indeed the first shot of Toba-Fushimi and so of the Boshin War. Contemporary accounts agree the Satsuma side fired first, a bursting shell throwing the shogunal column into confusion. Well attested.
